title: Little girl, get up (Mark 5:35–43)
hookLine: Mark keeps his Aramaic words, talitha koum, and then: give her something to eat
carry: care goes on to the kitchen

cards: While Jesus is still speaking to the woman, men come from Jairus's house with the news. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any more?
Picture Jairus's face. He did everything right. He begged, he hurried, and the delay for someone else's healing cost him everything.

Jesus overhears, turns to him, and says five words. Then he goes to the house anyway, where the mourners have already started wailing. And in that small room, Mark keeps Jesus's words in the language he said them in.

teach.b: The five words, in the old King James Bible: "Be not afraid, only believe." At the house, the crying is loud. Jesus says the child isn't dead but sleeping, and they laugh at him.
So he sends everyone out except her mother and father and three disciples, Peter, James and John.

teach.h: HE TOOK HER BY THE HAND.
teach.b: Then "he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise."
Mark wrote in Greek, but here he keeps the Aramaic words and translates them for his readers.

teach.h: TALITHA KOUM: LITTLE GIRL, GET UP.
teach.b: Talitha is a tender word, something like little girl. Koum means get up. It's what you might say to a child on a school morning.
No grand formula. Just her hand in his. And she gets up and walks around.
Mark adds, for she was twelve years old: the same twelve years the woman in the crowd had suffered. Then two closing lines, both so human. He tells them to keep it quiet.
And he "commanded that something should be given her to eat." The miracle ends with a snack. Christians read this as a sign of Jesus's power over death, and of the hope of resurrection.
Some readers treasure the ending too: after the impossible thing, the practical one. A child who's been very sick needs food. Care doesn't stop at the miracle.
It goes on to the kitchen.

how: Christians read this story as a sign of hope in the resurrection, and many congregations answer illness and grief with meals brought to the family's door.

o: a Hebrew blessing said over the sick
Aramaic for little girl, get up

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: it's Aramaic. Mark keeps it and translates it into Greek.
the girl was twelve years old
the same twelve years the woman in the crowd had been ill.
Jesus let the whole crowd watch
he sent them out, keeping only the parents and Peter, James and John.

games.q: you're Jairus. while Jesus stopped for someone else, word comes: your daughter is dead. don't trouble him any more. what does Jesus say?
o: I'm sorry. I came too late.
games.why: be not afraid, only believe. then he goes to the house, takes her hand and says: talitha koum.

practice: Hear it gently: talitha koum, little girl, get up, said to a child with her hand held.

Now think of someone who needs to get up from something, an illness, a grief, a long bad season, and ask the practical question Jesus asked: what do they need to eat, a meal you could bring, a coffee, a snack to share?
If you pray, you can hold them before God as you think it through.

wordCard.voice: Talitha koum. Aramaic for little girl, get up. Mark kept the sound of it, then translated it.

orig.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters by Mark: little girl, get up. Some manuscripts read koumi.

carryVoice: Your line: care goes on to the kitchen. Her hand in his, and then a plate. Day one hundred seventy-nine, done.
